title: Building Lightweight Vector Search in PostgreSQL with pgvector for Real-Time Semantic Recommendations
seoTitle: Lightweight Vector Search with PostgreSQL & pgvector
description: Learn how to build fast semantic recommendations using PostgreSQL and pgvector without third-party vector databases or complex microservices.

author.name: Aafaque Nazir
author.bio: Independent web engineer building high-performance websites, e-commerce stores, and SaaS web applications for clients across India & worldwide.

quickAnswer: pgvector enables vector similarity search directly inside your relational PostgreSQL database using cosine or L2 distance. Storing text embeddings in a standard table allows you to query semantic recommendations in single-digit milliseconds alongside typical relational filters, eliminating the operational cost of dedicated vector engines.

faqs.question: Why use pgvector instead of a standalone vector database like Pinecone?
faqs.answer: pgvector lives directly inside your primary relational database. This allows you to join vector search results directly with real-time stock levels, user permissions, and price filters in a single query. It eliminates data sync lag and lowers infrastructure bills by avoiding a second managed service.

faqs.question: Which indexing method should I use: HNSW or IVFFlat?
faqs.answer: Use HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) for almost all production web apps. It offers significantly higher queries per second and better recall without requiring you to rebuild the index as your dataset grows, unlike IVFFlat which needs periodic retraining.

faqs.question: How fast are pgvector queries on modest cloud servers?
faqs.answer: On a database with tens of thousands of products and an HNSW index, cosine distance queries run in 5ms to 15ms. That speed is fast enough to run dynamic product recommendations on live product detail pages without caching.

sections.title: The Problem with Dedicated Vector Databases

sections.text: Many startups jump immediately to external vector databases when building AI features. While specialized tools work well for multi-million vector datasets, they introduce unnecessary complexity for typical web applications. Managing two databases means synchronizing product changes, handling eventual consistency bugs, and paying two monthly invoices.

When building e-commerce catalogs like [Shopease / Oud & Attar](/projects/2/), recommendations must respect stock status, regional catalog availability, and category rules. If your vectors live in an external tool, you must query vectors first, extract IDs, and then query PostgreSQL to filter out out-of-stock items. With pgvector, this entire flow runs inside a single, fast SQL statement.

sections.title: Configuring pgvector and HNSW in PostgreSQL

sections.text: To get started, enable the extension and define a vector column on your catalog table. For OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small model, the vector dimension is 1536.

sections.caption: PostgreSQL schema with pgvector and HNSW index
sections.code:
-- 1. Enable the pgvector extension
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- 2. Add an embedding column to your products table
ALTER TABLE products 
ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS embedding vector(1536);

-- 3. Create an HNSW index for cosine distance queries
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS products_embedding_hnsw_idx 
ON products 
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

-- 4. Fast RPC function for similarity search with stock filtering
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION match_related_products (
  target_embedding vector(1536),
  match_threshold float,
  match_count int,
  current_product_id bigint
)
RETURNS TABLE (
  id bigint,
  name text,
  slug text,
  price numeric,
  similarity float
)
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
AS $$
  SELECT
    p.id,
    p.name,
    p.slug,
    p.price,
    1 - (p.embedding <=> target_embedding) AS similarity
  FROM products p
  WHERE p.id <> current_product_id
    AND p.is_in_stock = true
    AND 1 - (p.embedding <=> target_embedding) > match_threshold
  ORDER BY p.embedding <=> target_embedding
  LIMIT match_count;
$$;

sections.title: Index Choice Insight
sections.text: The operator <=> calculates cosine distance. In pgvector, cosine distance equals 1 minus the cosine similarity. An HNSW index using vector_cosine_ops allows your queries to scale to hundreds of thousands of rows while keeping query execution times well under 20 milliseconds.

items: Store the vector output directly in your products row so you do not need to re-encode the active item on every view.
Use HNSW index parameters (m = 16, ef_construction = 64) for balanced memory usage and index build times.
Always combine vector distance with practical SQL WHERE clauses like inventory counts and active flags.
Set maintenance_work_mem appropriately when building large indexes so PostgreSQL does not write intermediate sorting pages to disk.
